{{Short description|Mathematic orthonornal wavelet}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Strömberg wavelet''' is a certain [[orthonormal wavelet]] discovered by Jan-Olov Strömberg and presented in a paper published in 1983.<ref name=Stromberg>Janos-Olov Strömberg, ''A modified Franklin system and higher order spline systems on R<sup>n</sup> as unconditional bases for [[Hardy space]]s'', Conference on Harmonic Analysis in Honor of A. Zygmond, Vol. II, W. Beckner, et al (eds.) Wadsworth, 1983, pp.475-494</ref>  Even though the [[Haar wavelet]] was earlier known to be an orthonormal wavelet, Strömberg wavelet was the first smooth orthonormal wavelet to be discovered. The term  ''wavelet'' had not been coined at the time of publishing the discovery of Strömberg wavelet and Strömberg's motivation was to find an orthonormal basis for the [[Hardy space]]s.<ref name=Stromberg/>

==Definition==
Let ''m'' be any [[non-negative integer]]. Let ''V'' be any [[discrete subset]] of the set ''R'' of [[real number]]s. Then ''V'' splits ''R'' into non-overlapping [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]]s. For any ''r'' in ''V'', let ''I''<sub>''r''</sub> denote the interval determined by ''V'' with ''r'' as the left endpoint. Let ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''V'') denote the set of all [[Function (mathematics)|function]]s ''f''(''t'') over ''R'' satisfying the following conditions:
:*''f''(''t'') is [[square integrable]].
:*''f''(''t'') has [[Continuity (mathematics)|continuous]] [[derivative]]s of all orders up to ''m''.
:*''f''(''t'') is a [[polynomial]] of degree ''m'' + 1 in each of the intervals ''I''<sub>''r''</sub>.
If ''A''<sub>0</sub> =  {. . . , -2, -3/2, -1, -1/2} &cup; {0} &cup; {1, 2, 3, . . .} and ''A''<sub>1</sub> = ''A''<sub>0</sub> &cup; { 1/2 } then the '''Strömberg wavelet''' of order ''m'' is a function ''S''<sup>''m''</sup>(''t'') satisfying the following conditions:<ref name=Stromberg/>
:* <math>S^m(t)\in P^{(m)} (A_1).</math>
:*<math>\Vert S^m(t)\Vert=1</math>, that is, <math>\int_R\vert S^m(t)\vert^2\, dt = 1.</math>
:* <math>S^m(t)</math> is [[orthogonal]] to <math>P^{(m)}(A_0)</math>,  that is, <math>\int_R S^m(t)\, f(t)\, dt=0</math> for all <math>f(t)\in P^{(m)}(A_0).</math>

=== Properties of the set ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''V'') ===
The following are some of the properties of the set ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''V''):
# Let the number of distinct elements in ''V'' be two. Then ''f''(''t'') &isin; ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''V'') if and only if ''f''(''t'') = 0 for all ''t''.
# If the number of elements in ''V'' is three or more than ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''V'') contains nonzero functions.
# If ''V''<sub>1</sub> and ''V''<sub>2</sub> are discrete subsets of ''R'' such that ''V''<sub>1</sub> &sub; ''V''<sub>2</sub> then ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''V''<sub>1</sub>) &sub; ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''V''<sub>2</sub>). In particular, ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''A''<sub>0</sub>) &sub; ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''A''<sub>1</sub>).
# If ''f''(''t'') &isin; ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''A''<sub>1</sub>) then ''f''(''t'') = ''g''(''t'') + &alpha; &lambda;(''t'') where &alpha; is constant and ''g''(''t'') &isin; ''P''<sup>(''m'')</sup>(''A''<sub>0</sub>) is defined by ''g''(''r'') = ''f''(''r'') for ''r'' &isin; ''A''<sub>0</sub>.

=== Strömberg wavelet as an orthonormal wavelet ===
The following result establishes the Strömberg wavelet as an [[orthonormal wavelet]].<ref name=Stromberg/>

=== Theorem ===
Let ''S''<sup>''m''</sup> be the Strömberg wavelet of order ''m''. Then the following set
::<math>\left\{2^{j/2}S^m(2^jt-k):j,k \text{ integers }\right\}</math>
is a complete [[orthonormal]] system in the space of square integrable functions over ''R''.

==Strömberg wavelets of order 0==
[[File:StrombergWaveletOfOrderZero.png|thumb|400px|right|The graph of the Strömberg wavelet of order 0. The graph is scaled such that the value of the wavelet function at 1 is 1.]]

In the special case of Strömberg wavelets of order 0, the following facts may be observed:
# If ''f''(''t'') &isin; ''P''<sup>0</sup>(''V'') then ''f''(''t'') is defined uniquely by the discrete subset {''f''(''r'') : ''r'' &isin; ''V''} of ''R''.
# To each ''s'' &isin; ''A''<sub>0</sub>, a special function &lambda;<sub>''s''</sub> in ''A''<sub>0</sub> is associated: It is defined by &lambda;<sub>''s''</sub>(''r'') = 1 if ''r'' = ''s'' and &lambda;<sub>''s''</sub>(''r'') = 0 if  ''s'' &ne; ''r'' &isin; ''A''<sub>0</sub>. These special elements in ''P''(''A''<sub>0</sub>) are called ''simple tents''. The special simple tent &lambda;<sub>1/2</sub>(''t'') is denoted by &lambda;(''t'')

=== Computation of the Strömberg wavelet of order 0 ===
As already observed, the Strömberg wavelet ''S''<sup>0</sup>(''t'') is completely determined by the set { ''S''<sup>0</sup>(''r'') : ''r'' &isin; ''A''<sub>1</sub> }. Using the defining properties of the Strömbeg wavelet, exact expressions for elements of this set can be computed and they are given below.<ref name=Woj>{{cite book|last1=P. Wojtaszczyk|title=A Mathematical Introduction to Wavelets|url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicalintr00wojt|url-access=registration|date=1997|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=0521570204|pages=[https://archive.org/details/mathematicalintr00wojt/page/n14 5]–14}}</ref>
::<math> S^0(k) = S^0(1)(\sqrt{3}-2)^{k-1}</math> for <math> k=1,2,3, \ldots</math>
::<math>S^0(\tfrac{1}{2})  =  -S^0(1)\left(\sqrt{3}+\tfrac{1}{2}\right)</math>
::<math>S^0(0) = S^0(1)(2\sqrt{3}-2)</math>
::<math>S^0(-\tfrac{k}{2}) = S^0(1)(2\sqrt{3}-2)(\sqrt{3}-2)^k</math> for <math>k=1,2,3, \ldots</math>
Here ''S''<sup>0</sup>(1) is constant such that ||''S''<sup>0</sup>(''t'')||&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.

=== Some additional information about Strömberg wavelet of order 0 ===
The Strömberg wavelet of order 0 has the following properties.<ref name=Woj/>
:*The Strömberg wavelet ''S''<sup>0</sup>(''t'') [[oscillation|oscillates]] about ''t''-axis.
:*The Strömberg wavelet ''S''<sup>0</sup>(''t'') has [[exponential decay]]. 
:*The values of  ''S''<sup>0</sup>(''t'') for positive integral values of ''t'' and for negative half-integral values of ''t'' are related as follows: <math>S^0(-k/2)=(10-6\sqrt{3})S^0(k)</math> for <math>k=1,2,3,\ldots\,.</math>
